meaning: A friendly way to ask how someone is.
usageNote: Use it to greet friends or coworkers you know. Answer with "Good, thanks!"
examples: Morning, Lee. How's it going with the new laptop?
How's it going? I haven't seen you all week.

meaning: Goodbye — I will see you again soon.
usageNote: Use it when you leave and expect to see the person again, today or soon.
examples: Thanks for lunch! See you later.
I'm off to the meeting. See you later.

meaning: A strong, warm way to say thanks.
usageNote: Use it when someone helped you a lot or did something kind.
examples: Thank you so much for the flowers!
Thank you so much for your quick reply.
You fixed my bike? Thank you so much!

meaning: A polite way to say goodbye and wish someone well.
usageNote: Common in shops, cafés, and at the end of short conversations.
examples: Here's your coffee. Have a nice day!
Bye, Ana! Have a nice day.
Thanks for calling, and have a nice day.

meaning: Stop working or studying for a short time to rest.
usageNote: We say "take" a break, not "make" a break.
examples: Let's take a break and get some water.
We'll take a break at eleven and continue after.
You look tired. Take a break!

meaning: Used to add a new topic or extra information.
usageNote: Use it to change the topic naturally, often at the start of a sentence.
examples: By the way, I loved your photos.
By the way, the report is due on Friday.
By the way, did you call Mike?

meaning: Choose what to do after thinking about it.
usageNote: We "make" a decision, not "do" a decision.
examples: I can't make a decision about the dress.
We need to make a decision before Monday.
Take your time to make a decision.

meaning: I feel excited about something in the future.
usageNote: Use it when you are happy about a plan. "To" is followed by a noun or "-ing" verb.
examples: The trip is next week. I'm looking forward to it!
Thanks for the invitation. I'm looking forward to it.
A concert on Saturday? I'm looking forward to it.

meaning: It's fine — it was easy or I'm happy to help.
usageNote: Use it to answer "thank you" or "sorry" in a relaxed way.
examples: Can you send it again? — No problem, here it is.

meaning: Watch, listen, or think carefully about something.
usageNote: Usually followed by "to": pay attention to the details.
examples: Pay attention to the road, please.
Please pay attention to the new safety rules.
I wasn't paying attention. Can you repeat that?

meaning: I understand your reason, and it seems logical.
usageNote: Use it to show you understand someone's reason, idea, or explanation.
examples: Oh, you took the earlier train? That makes sense.
The deadline moved because of the launch. That makes sense.
You prefer mornings when it's quiet? That makes sense.

text: at the end of the day
meaning: When you think about what really matters.
usageNote: Use it to give your final, most important point.
examples: At the end of the day, you have to be happy.
At the end of the day, the client decides.
It's expensive, but at the end of the day it's worth it.

meaning: I usually do something; it's my habit.
usageNote: Follow it with a base verb: I tend to wake up early.
examples: I tend to drink tea in the evening.
I tend to reply to emails in the morning.
I tend to forget names, sorry!

meaning: Become familiar with something new until it feels normal.
usageNote: Follow it with a noun or an "-ing" verb: get used to working from home.
examples: It took me a month to get used to the cold.
You'll get used to the new system quickly.
I can't get used to waking up at six.

meaning: Approximately — it might not be exactly this.
usageNote: Put it at the end when you aren't sure of the exact word or number.
examples: She works in marketing or something like that.
The meeting is at three or something like that.
Let's get pizza or something like that.

meaning: Even so; despite what I just said.
usageNote: Use it to add a contrasting point after a statement.
examples: The hotel was small. Having said that, it was very clean.
Sales fell this year. Having said that, profits are up.
I'm tired. Having said that, I'd love to come.

meaning: Think of an idea, plan, or answer.
usageNote: Usually followed by a noun: come up with a plan, an idea, a name.
examples: We need to come up with a name for the dog.
Can the team come up with a better solution?
She always comes up with funny stories.

meaning: Used to introduce a different side of an argument.
usageNote: Often used after "On the one hand..." to compare two ideas.
examples: The city is exciting. On the other hand, it's very expensive.
Option A is cheaper. On the other hand, option B is faster.
I want to go out. On the other hand, I need sleep.

meaning: Something is not difficult for me to do.
usageNote: Follow it with a base verb. Change "easy" to "hard" for the opposite.
examples: I find it easy to talk to new people.
I find it easy to work with clear deadlines.
I find it easy to cook for my family.

meaning: And other similar things.
usageNote: Use it at the end of a list instead of naming every item.
examples: I like hiking, camping, and that kind of thing.
We handle invoices, refunds, and that kind of thing.
She sells candles, soap, and that kind of thing.

meaning: Tell a secret, often by accident.
usageNote: Informal. Use it about surprises or secret news.
examples: Don't spill the beans about the party!
Someone spilled the beans about the merger.
Come on, spill the beans! Who is he?

meaning: In general; mostly.
usageNote: Use it to give an overall opinion while admitting exceptions.
examples: By and large, the trip was fun.
By and large, customers are happy with the service.
The movie was, by and large, a success.

meaning: Consider something when making a decision.
usageNote: The object can go in the middle: take your budget into account.
examples: Did you take into account the traffic?
We must take into account the new regulations.
Take into account that she's only five.

meaning: Very different from something.
usageNote: Use it to compare two things that are very different, often worse or better.
examples: This tiny flat is a far cry from our old house.
The results are a far cry from what we expected.
My cooking is a far cry from my mom's.

meaning: Remember something important while you decide or act.
usageNote: Often used as advice: Bear in mind that...
examples: Bear in mind that the shop closes at six.
Please bear in mind that prices may change.
Bear in mind he's new here.

meaning: In every important way; practically.
usageNote: Formal. Use it when something is almost completely true.
examples: To all intents and purposes, the holiday is over.
To all intents and purposes, the project is finished.
The car is, to all intents and purposes, new.

meaning: Something with both good and bad effects.
usageNote: Use it to show that an advantage also brings a risk.
examples: Living close to work is a double-edged sword.
Fast growth can be a double-edged sword.

meaning: The most important thing, the only thing that matters.
usageNote: Often used in the negative: Money isn't the be-all and end-all.
examples: Grades aren't the be-all and end-all.
Price is not the be-all and end-all for our buyers.
For him, football is the be-all and end-all.

text: in the grand scheme of things
meaning: When you think about the whole situation.
usageNote: Use it to say a problem is small compared with the bigger picture.
examples: In the grand scheme of things, one bad day isn't a big deal.
In the grand scheme of things, the delay is minor.
In the grand scheme of things, it doesn't matter.

meaning: Find a fair middle point between two different needs.
usageNote: Usually followed by "between": strike a balance between work and rest.
examples: I'm trying to strike a balance between work and fun.
We must strike a balance between speed and quality.
It's hard to strike a balance with two kids.
